notes.meaning: Solomon took thirteen years to build his royal palace complex, nearly twice the time he spent on the temple. He built God's house first and without delay, while he took his time on his own residence. Putting the Lord's house ahead of his own comfort showed proper honor to God.

differ.view: Solomon spending thirteen years on his palace shows that his personal priorities had begun to slip away from wholehearted devotion to God.

notes.meaning: Solomon built a massive hall called the House of the Forest of Lebanon. It earned this name because of its many tall cedar pillars, which looked like a forest. The building was about one hundred and fifty feet long and served as a royal armory and public hall.

The roof of the hall was made of fragrant cedar wood placed over crossbeams. These beams rested on forty-five cedar pillars arranged in rows of fifteen. This sturdy wooden framework supported the upper rooms of the building.

The building had three rows of windows placed directly opposite each other on three levels. This allowed daylight to flow straight through the hall. It also gave matching views from both sides of the building.
All the doors and doorposts had rectangular, squared frames instead of arches. The doorways lined up across from each other on all three levels. This orderly design matched the rows of windows.

Solomon built a porch of pillars seventy-five feet long and forty-five feet wide. In front of it stood another covered entry porch with its own pillars and steps. This area provided a grand waiting space for people visiting the king on official business.

Solomon built a special judgment hall where his royal throne was placed. Here the king listened to legal appeals and gave verdicts in person. The room was paneled with cedar wood from the floor to the ceiling to mark the dignity of royal justice.

Behind the public judgment hall, Solomon built his own private palace with a similar design. He also constructed a matching residence for his wife, the daughter of Pharaoh. These personal quarters were finished with the same fine cedar craftsmanship.

All these royal buildings were made from top-grade stones cut carefully to measure. Stonemasons trimmed the blocks with saws on both the inside and outside faces. This high quality ran from the underground foundations up to the roof beams.

The foundation was laid with massive, costly stones measuring twelve to fifteen feet in length. Solomon did not cut corners on the parts hidden underground. He gave the palace the strongest possible base.

Above the heavy foundation stones, the builders laid high-grade cut stone and sturdy cedar beams. The walls rose with the same care and expensive materials throughout. Everything was crafted to the exact measurements required.

The large courtyard around the palace had a wall made of three layers of cut stone topped by cedar beams. This matched the design of the courtyard surrounding the Lord's temple. Solomon patterned his own courts after the house of God.

King Solomon sent messengers to bring a master craftsman named Huram from the city of Tyre. This man was not the king of Tyre, but an expert in bronze metalwork. Solomon hired him to direct the metal casting for the temple.

Huram's mother was an Israelite widow from the tribe of Naphtali, and his deceased father had been a Tyrian bronze worker. Huram possessed great talent, intelligence, and skill in casting bronze. He traveled to Jerusalem and completed all the metal tasks Solomon assigned to him.

Huram cast two huge hollow bronze pillars for the temple. Each pillar stood about twenty-seven feet tall and measured about eighteen feet around. They were monumental columns made to stand in front of the temple entrance.

Huram cast two bronze capitals, or ornamental tops, to sit on the pillars. Each capital was five cubits high, which is about seven and a half feet tall. These heavy bronze crowns completed the top of each column.

Huram decorated each capital with a network of lattice and seven woven bronze chains. These chains hung like festoons or wreaths around the rounded lower part of the capital. They added rich texture and beauty to the metalwork.

He crafted two rows of bronze pomegranates around the chainwork on each capital. These fruit shapes encircled the columns above and below the woven lattice. In Israel, pomegranates served as a familiar symbol of rich blessing and fruitful life.

The upper part of each capital was shaped like an open lily flower about six feet high. This floral design crowned the very top of each column. It brought a soft and graceful appearance to the massive bronze pillars.

Each capital held two hundred bronze pomegranates arranged in two even rows around the bowl-shaped curve. This brought the total to four hundred pomegranates on the two pillars. The careful spacing made both columns look balanced and complete.

Huram placed the two pillars at the entrance porch of the temple. He named the south pillar Jachin, meaning 'He will establish,' and the north pillar Boaz, meaning 'In Him is strength.' The pillars supported no roof, but reminded worshippers that God alone gives strength and stability to His people.

With the lily-shaped metal tops in place, the work on the twin pillars was finished. They stood at the temple entrance as lasting reminders of God's power and beauty. The priests and people passed between them whenever they came to worship.

Huram cast an enormous round bronze basin called the Sea. It measured about fifteen feet across the rim, seven and a half feet high, and forty-five feet around. It was called a 'Sea' because of the vast amount of water it held for temple cleansing.

Under the outer rim of the basin ran two rows of carved bronze buds shaped like wild gourds. There were ten of these ornaments per cubit all the way around the bowl. They were cast in one piece with the basin itself rather than attached later.

The giant basin rested on the backs of twelve bronze oxen. Three oxen faced north, three west, three south, and three east, with their tails pointed toward the center. The twelve oxen represented the twelve tribes of Israel coming to God for cleansing, as well as patient strength in service.

The bronze walls of the basin were about three inches thick, and the rim flared outward like a blooming lily cup. It held several thousand gallons of water. The priests used this water to wash their hands and feet so they would be clean when serving God.
